title: Welcome to OS DataMercs
description: OS DataMercs is inspired to elevate the publishing industry by consulting, teaching and providing most recognized metadata services.
contents:
Contents
// Trinity of Discovery

// Trinity of Discovery
The “Trinity of Discovery” exhibits our holistic approach to metadata delivery and creation, and sets the framework to a title’s - may it be eBook or journal - (meta) data needs.
It is also what most libraries would expect to receive from a publisher one way or another, either directly or through third party services or union catalogues:
Meta data and discovery from the smallest chunk down to collection level, because

»We are not going to buy any of your eBooks if users cannot discover them!«
(an unnamed head of aqcuisition)

MARC records, KBARTs, ONIX and JATS XML are key, and even sales relevant, especially to scientific publishing houses!
Naturally, one could go beyond that, if we talked about linked data, which would even aim at the most atomic bits of data points, but since most publishers usually have hardly even the basics covered, the trinity shall serve as our North star here.
Guided by “Five Laws of Library Science” (published by Shiyali Ramainrita (S. R.) Ranganathan (1892-1972), an Indian mathematician and library science scholar, in 19311), which are:

Books are for use.
Every person his or her book!
Every book its reader.
Save the time of the reader.
A Library is a growing organism.

this site aims to showcase several tools and workflows around that, so that even the smallest publisher, or inclined librarian, can build upon that and implement their own (half-) automated data pipelines, From ERP to .MRC;-)

title: Paying twice for prestige
description: Open Access Week 2026 asks about "The Cost of Knowledge". In Germany the cost is published per article. Why libraries and university presses do not simply publish themselves: the infrastructure exists, the incentives do not. Homework for appointment committees, university presses, library networks and the DFG.
contents:
Open Access Week has chosen “The Cost of Knowledge” as its theme for 19 to 25 October, which is generous of it, since in Germany the cost is published per article. A researcher writes a paper, gives it to a publisher, reviews someone else’s for free, and the university then pays between €2,200 and €3,150 for it to appear openly, plus reading access to the rest of the journal list.
The conscious librarian asks why libraries and university presses do not simply do this themselves.
The polite answer is that they already can. The less polite answer, and this is our view, is that nobody is promoted for it.
Who does what, on which layer
Before anyone is blamed, it helps to know what each party was built to do.
DEAL is a national licensing contract, not a publishing strategy. It turns subscription money into “publish and read” fees: €2,600 per article at Springer Nature, €3,150, €2,700 or €2,200 by journal tier at Wiley, and €2,500 at Elsevier in the first year, after 90% participation earned a 2% discount.
The DFG’s publication-cost programme is a subsidy meant to change how money flows. It pays a flat €1,400 per article and €5,000 per book, takes its last applications in 2027, and gives way to a successor programme with a first deadline of 4 May 2027.
SeDOA is the service layer: a DFG-funded national centre for fee-free Diamond journals, approved on 11 December 2024 and run by 15 institutions under ULB Darmstadt, with the AG Universitätsverlage directly involved.
The Action Plan for Diamond Open Access is the coordination layer. It names efficiency, quality standards, capacity building and sustainability, and calls the sector an “archipelago of relatively isolated journals and platforms”.
The AG Universitätsverlage quality standards are the floor for open-access books, which the DFG already treats as binding for the books it funds. We read version 3 in “Quality is a column, not a vibe”.
DORA, CoARA and the DFG CV form the assessment layer. The DFG signed DORA in 2021, is a CoARA signatory, and since March 2023 has limited CVs to ten publications plus ten other outputs such as data, software and preprints.
Each of these does roughly what it says on the tin. The difficulty is the tin they are all standing in.
What the money buys
DEAL did what it was built to do. The institutions taking part account for about 90% of German output in the three publishers’ journals, and the contracts could move around half of Germany’s journal output to open access. That is real access, and nobody should pretend otherwise.
What it does not change is who supplies the labour: Authors write, colleagues review and editors edit, mostly at no charge, and the institution then pays for everyone to read the result.
Paying twice is not fraud. It is simply what a market looks like when the customer also supplies the goods. The DFG’s €1,400 covers part of the fee; the institution covers the rest.
Why presses do not win by default
Building an alternative is not the hard part. SeDOA, the Action Plan and the AG standards already exist. The hard part is that a fee-free journal at a university press must compete for authors whose careers are decided by appointment panels.
A press can, however, take over a prestige title. The Gutenberg-Jahrbuch, published since 1926 for the International Gutenberg Society in Mainz, is moving to Diamond Open Access with Heidelberg University Publishing (heiUP): CC BY-SA 4.0, no fees for authors or readers, OJS and an XML-first workflow, with the backfiles of the previous 100 yearbooks to be digitised. The project runs from 1 October 2026 (Archivalia). Gutenberg, one gathers, has survived worse changes of format.
The DFG has reformed its own reviewing. CoARA, however, binds each signatory’s own processes, not every faculty in the country. One notices that a ten-publication CV still leaves open the question of which ten, and that question remains available to be read off the masthead.
Diamond publishing has a cost problem of its own. The cOAlition S Diamond journals study (2021) found that 86% of Diamond journals publish fewer than 50 articles a year, 60% depend on volunteers, and almost a third did not know their financial status.
“Free to read and to publish in” is not the same as “costs nothing”; someone is paying, usually in evenings.
So, to the founder’s question: it is not mainly immobility, nor mainly author vanity - it is a reward system that prices the brand, and a set of public bodies too polite to put that price in a single table.
Homework
Appointment and tenure committees, at each university, before the next round.
If DORA, CoARA and the DFG CV are the assessment layer already on the table, the minimal operational step is to adopt the DFG CV format, keep journal impact factors out of job calls and assessment, and record in the minutes that this was done. Where a university has not signed CoARA, it is perhaps worth recording either the signature or the reason for its absence.
University presses, before 4 May 2027.
If the AG standards are the floor the DFG already treats as binding, then a public statement of which required items are met is the natural next column. Ship the CC0 metadata licence in a feed that actually exists (ONIX 3, OAI-PMH or MARC, as the standards name them), not only as a sentence on a web page. Switch on a DOI link checker. Register journals and series with SeDOA.
Library networks, every year.
If DEAL is a licensing contract and Diamond is the service layer, the two sides of the ledger belong in one public table. Publish DEAL invoices alongside Diamond and press budgets, set a target share for Diamond, and report against it.
The DFG, by the time the successor programme starts paying in 2028.
If the publication-cost programme was meant to change how money flows, the successor can record the split between per-article fees and institutional Diamond infrastructure. Publish a list of presses that meet the required AG items, rather than accepting a PDF as the audit.
Close
None of this requires a revolution, only a spreadsheet! Prestige is a line item; it merely happens to be filed under someone else’s budget. Put it in ours, where it can be audited, and the bill may start to shrink.
The German Open Access Week programme is at open-access.network. The SeDOA sessions are on Wednesday 21 October, from 13:00 Berlin time.

title: News wrap · 19 October 2026 - Labelled for machines
description: Weekly news wrap (not a workshop) for 19 October 2026. In Dublin, the European Commission revises its research guidance on generative AI, now with a chapter on AI agents and peer review, and collects first pledges from Elsevier, Frontiers and others; EDItEUR’s ONIX codelists gain a content audience for LLM training; a Scholarly Kitchen guest post asks for evidence before more adoption; and in Japan, NII documents how its open LLM-jp-4 models were built, with a rights level for every dataset, while the Humanitext project turns AI suggestions into expert-verified, sourced links.
contents:
Industry notes · news wrap · not a workshop


Week of 19 October 2026


A briefing of what to notice this week, with sources. How-to and cataloguing practice stay in separate posts — see Ghost in the MARC for the standards work.

Last week the trade asked whether an AI answer can say where it came from. This week the question moved one layer down, to the label on the package itself.
In Dublin, the European Commission revised its guidance on generative AI in research, now with explicit rules of thumb for AI agents and peer review, and collected the first private pledges for AI in European science.
EDItEUR’s new ONIX codelists give publishers a way to say, in metadata, “this text is meant for machines”.
And in Japan, the National Institute of Informatics published a training report in which every dataset carries a rights level.
The courier rule still applies: whatever is not written on the label will be guessed at the other end.
Dublin: the guidance grows an agent chapter
What happened. On 15 October, at the European AI in Science Summit in Dublin, the Commission launched the RAISE pledging initiative for AI in Science Enablers, which collects in-kind support for European researchers from industry and philanthropy. First commitments came from the Novo Nordisk Foundation, Nvidia, Elsevier, Sanofi, Frontiers, Mistral and Google DeepMind. Pledges are to show support “beyond their direct commercial interests” and will be reviewed annually (Commission press release IP/26/2175, 15 Oct; RAISE pledging page).
Two of the first pledgers are publishers:
Elsevier offers 4,000 complimentary licences (1,000 each for LeapSpace, ClinicalKey AI, ClinicalKey Nursing AI and Complete Anatomy) and an estimated €1m a year of in-kind support and funding. That covers at least three new research collaborations a year, a new Centre on Hybrid Intelligence for Trustworthy Research with the University of Amsterdam and Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, and training for about ten PhD candidates, postdocs and master’s students a year (Elsevier, 15 Oct).
Frontiers offers AI-powered curation for 1,000 Horizon Europe datasets and 100 FAIR² Data Publication Grants for early-career researchers. The pledge is described as more than €1.6 million in services, free to researchers, and Frontiers offers its FAIR² open specification for institutions, repositories and infrastructures to adopt (RAISE pledging page).
At the same summit, the Commission presented the fourth version of the ERA Living Guidelines on the responsible use of generative AI in research, which it calls the most comprehensive update since the first version in 2024 (DG RTD news, 16 Oct; guidelines PDF).
The intended layer. This is a non-binding stakeholder document from the ERA Forum, addressed to researchers, research organisations and research funders. It says outright that it adds no new requirements; it translates existing research-integrity principles to a workflow that now includes AI. Publishers and libraries are named as part of the conversation, but the recommendations are not written for them. Read it as the expectations your authors, reviewers and funders will bring to you, not as a rulebook for your production desk.
What is new and useful.
Agents. AI agents are “advanced research tools, not independent scientists”. Using an agent “may never be considered a delegation of control or responsibility”, and researchers should build in checkpoints where critical decisions, such as methodological ones, are validated by a person.
Disclosure. Researchers disclose AI tools used substantially, describe what they did, and describe oversight and verification. A footnote draws a useful line: basic editorial support is not substantial; using AI for a literature review, to identify research gaps or to develop hypotheses is. Authors decide whether prompts, logs, model versions and parameters should be kept or shared, based on whether they are needed to understand, reproduce or audit the work.
Peer review. The judgement of scientific quality and merit is not delegated to AI. Reviewers use only “secure, trusted tools”, preferably ones provided by the institution, funder or publisher, and should not upload unpublished material to systems that cannot guarantee confidentiality and non-use for training.
Hidden prompts. Funders are told to watch for instructions hidden in proposals, defined as text placed “through invisible text, formatting tricks, or metadata” that a person may not notice but an AI tool may still process.
The guidelines also point to the ISC, COPE, STM and Global Young Academy work on a global AI-disclosure standard, which will inform future versions. The next revision is planned for the third quarter of 2027.
Supplements for the metadata desk. The guidance stops at principles, as its layer should. Here is what we would add on the publishing side.
1. A disclosure record you can actually harvest. If authors are asked to describe substantive AI use and verification, give them fields rather than a free-text box. A minimal set:
Field
Example value
Why
ai_tool
product name as shown to the user
identifies the system
ai_version
version or date string
outputs differ between versions
task
controlled list: literature review / data analysis / translation / code / other
matches the guidelines’ “substantial use” examples
substantive
yes / no
the threshold the guidelines use
verified_by
ORCID iD of the responsible person
names the human who checked
verification_note
one sentence
how output was checked
records_kept
none / on request / deposited (with DOI)
prompts, logs, parameters
2. A hidden-prompt check at intake. Before any AI screener reads a submission, run a short audit: extract all text layers, including white or zero-size text and zero-width characters; read document properties and embedded XMP metadata; flag any imperative instructions aimed at a model. Log the result with the submission. The same check belongs in metadata ingestion: an abstract field is now an attack surface.
3. Four questions for any review-assistance vendor. Is our content used to train your models, and is that contractual? Which model version scored this manuscript, and is that logged per item? Do you strip hidden instructions before inference? Can editors see why a flag was raised?
The pledges themselves we welcome without irony. Free tool access and AI-ready datasets are acceleration, and Europe needs it. The useful check over the next year is the one the Commission has set itself: an annual review, with pledges and progress presented at future editions of the summit. Delivered access, not announced access, is what researchers will notice.
Standards & metadata: ONIX learns the word “LLM”
What changed. EDItEUR published Issue 75 of the ONIX for Books codelists in mid-October. The changes were ratified by the ONIX International Steering Committee at its meeting during the Frankfurt Book Fair, and the change summary is dated 7 October (Issue 75 changes, PDF; live codelist browser, List 154). The AI-relevant additions:
List 154 (Content audience), code 13 “LLM training”: material not intended for display, but which may be used “for AI training, GEO and RAG”. (Our glosses: GEO is usually read as generative engine optimisation, the AI-era cousin of search-engine optimisation; RAG is retrieval-augmented generation, where a model looks things up before it answers.)
List 158 (Resource content type), code 60 “LLM training data”: a data file specifically intended for those uses.
List 178 (Supporting resource file format), code D512 “JSON”, or JSON-LD.
List 153 (Text type), code 24: a schema.org snippet in JSON-LD.
EDItEUR’s note is careful about scope. These codes are for “initial exploratory use” of data in a special format that the German ONIX IG (the national user group) is to define. The linked data file sits apart from text meant for people, and any constraints or opt-outs on the book’s own content “should not be applied” to this file, because it is supplied specifically for AI use. Usage constraints can still be set for each supporting resource separately.
The intended layer. This is a controlled vocabulary for exchanging book-trade metadata, not a licence and not a payload format. It gives a sender a way to point at machine-only material and tell it apart from marketing copy. What that material contains is left, for now, to the German group. That is not a gap to complain about; it is the next work item, and DACH publishers have a direct line into it.
Two quieter additions matter to scholarly presses: List 163, codes 41 and 42, for the manuscript submission date and manuscript accepted date, “typically for academic and scholarly publishing”. Book metadata can now carry the same history dates that journal articles have long carried in JATS. In a week when disclosure standards ask when a work was reviewed, that is useful.
Supplements: a working checklist for an ONIX sender.
Decide what the “LLM training” text is: an extended abstract, a table of contents with chapter summaries, or nothing at all. Write it down as a house rule, not ad hoc per title.
Keep it consistent with your rights position. The text-and-data-mining code in List 145 (code 11), and the narrower private-AI codes 13 and 14 added in Issue 73, govern the book. The new resource is a separate decision. Record both decisions in the same place.
Version the file. Use the Last updated content date and a hash, so that a recipient, or an agent, can tell which version it used. List 162 already offers SHA-256 (code 08).
Ask your aggregators and retailers which of these codes they will actually read before you invest in producing the file.
An illustrative supporting-resource block (check element order against the ONIX 3.0 specification before use):
<SupportingResource>
  <ResourceContentType>60</ResourceContentType>   <!-- LLM training data -->
  <ContentAudience>13</ContentAudience>           <!-- LLM training -->
  <ResourceMode>04</ResourceMode>                 <!-- Text -->
  <ResourceVersion>
    <ResourceForm>02</ResourceForm>               <!-- Downloadable file -->
    <ResourceVersionFeature>
      <ResourceVersionFeatureType>01</ResourceVersionFeatureType>
      <FeatureValue>D512</FeatureValue>           <!-- JSON -->
    </ResourceVersionFeature>
    <ResourceVersionFeature>
      <ResourceVersionFeatureType>08</ResourceVersionFeatureType>
      <FeatureValue><!-- SHA-256 of the file --></FeatureValue>
    </ResourceVersionFeature>
    <ResourceLink>https://example.org/onix/9783000000000-llm.json</ResourceLink>
    <ContentDate>
      <ContentDateRole>17</ContentDateRole>       <!-- Last updated -->
      <Date>20261019</Date>
    </ContentDate>
  </ResourceVersion>
</SupportingResource>
What we would like the German format to carry, as a suggestion from the cheap seats: the work’s persistent identifiers (ISBN, DOI), the rightsholder, a licence statement in machine-readable form, the version of record it summarises, and who wrote the summary - a person, a model, or a model checked by a person. That last field is the disclosure question again, arriving through the back door of the book trade.
ONIX homework: who acts, on what, by when.
The layer first. The ONIX codelists are a technical standard. They are a shared vocabulary for book-trade metadata, not a licence and not a deadline. Issue 75 is dated 12 October 2026 (Issue 75 codelists). Every new code is optional. EDItEUR marks the LLM codes for “initial exploratory use” and sets no date by which recipients must read them. So there is no deadline. The practical one is before your next feed-schema update.
Publisher metadata team: load Issue 75 now. Update the codelist tables in your product-information system and your validator, so that List 154 code 13, List 158 code 60, List 178 code D512 and List 163 codes 41 and 42 validate. Loading codes commits you to nothing.
ONIX system owner (a Klopotek-type system, or your feed vendor): confirm the path before the next feed-schema update. Ask four questions.
Can the feed send <ContentAudience>13</ContentAudience> and <ResourceContentType>60</ResourceContentType> in a Block 2 <SupportingResource>?
Can it send <ResourceVersionFeatureType>01</ResourceVersionFeatureType> with <FeatureValue>D512</FeatureValue>?
Can it send the new date roles in <PublishingDate>?
And which release does the feed actually send: ONIX 3.0, or 3.1.1 or later?
Rights team, with the metadata team: make two decisions, not one. The book’s own text-and-data-mining position goes in Block 1 <EpubUsageConstraint>, using List 145 code 11 (or the narrower codes 13 and 14) with a List 146 status. EDItEUR says those book-level constraints should not be applied to the LLM-training file. Terms for that file go in its own <EpubUsageConstraint> inside the <SupportingResource>, and that placement needs ONIX 3.1.1 or later (ONIX 3.1.1 changes). If your feed is still on 3.0, it has nowhere to state terms for the file. Hold the file back until it does. Record both decisions in the same rights record.
Scholarly programme and metadata team: map the manuscript dates at the next change to your editorial system. Use List 163 code 41 (manuscript submission date) and code 42 (manuscript accepted date) in <PublishingDate>. These dates come from your submission and review system, not from ONIX. The work is mapping that field, not retyping it.
Metadata lead: watch the German ONIX IG, and do not build the payload yet. The format of the LLM-training file is still to be defined there. We found no published draft as of 18 October 2026. When a draft appears, pilot it on a handful of titles, with a SHA-256 hash (List 162 code 08) and a Last updated date on every version. Before you go further, ask your main recipients which of these codes they will actually ingest, and from when.
On the journal side, two dates for the diary. Crossref’s annual meeting and board election is online on 22 October, with an in-depth update on the new Member Practices on the agenda (Crossref). On 3 November, a Crossref webinar with Patricia Feeney, Liz Allen and Mike Nason looks at bringing the NISO CRediT and JAV recommendations into Crossref metadata, and “what implementation actually involves” (CRediT, 17 Oct).
Evidence desk: measure before you multiply
In a Scholarly Kitchen guest post on 14 October, Sarah Hands (Chief Operating Officer, PA EDitorial) argues that AI adoption in editorial workflows may be running ahead of the evidence. She is explicit that this is not resistance. Her concern is that success is measured too narrowly (speed and throughput), that wider costs show up elsewhere in the workflow, and that automation bias makes a system flag feel more authoritative than a colleague’s judgement. Her test: “An AI-generated flag isn’t necessarily a finding; it is a signal requiring context and interpretation.” She asks publishers to share null and negative results, not only successes (Scholarly Kitchen, 14 Oct).
The intended layer. An opinion piece from a service provider, not a policy. It sets out questions and leaves the measurement design to the reader, which is fair for the format.
Supplement: a one-page evaluation sheet for any AI step in an editorial or metadata workflow.
Baseline first. Record current error rates and turnaround for the task before you switch the tool on.
Adjudicated sample. For a fixed sample each month, a person decides independently. Count false positives and false negatives against that decision, not against the tool’s own confidence.
Disagreement log. Every case where the editor overrules the flag, or follows a flag that turns out wrong, gets one line. That log is your automation-bias detector.
Split by population. Report results by discipline, article type and first language of authors; averages hide exactly what Hands is worried about.
Downstream cost. Track the extra work created later: queries, appeals, corrections.
Review date. Every tool gets a date on which it is kept, changed or switched off, with the sheet attached.
Publish the sheet, even when the result is “inconclusive”. We are in favour of moving fast; we would just like to know where we are going.
Global desk: Japan publishes the recipe, and a line from China
Japan - a training report with rights levels. On 14 October, the LLM-jp team, coordinated by the National Institute of Informatics (NII), posted the technical report for LLM-jp-4, an 8B dense and a 32B-A3B mixture-of-experts model trained from scratch on about 12 trillion tokens and released under Apache 2.0 (arXiv:2610.19331). What makes it relevant to publishers is not the benchmark table but section 2, the selection rules:
Every dataset subset carries a release level from L1 to LZ, set out as yes/no columns for internal-model training, public-model training, retrieval (showing parts of the data to users) and redistribution. Only L1-L3 data were used for the public models.
The team requires that a dataset’s original construction was lawful, not only its own use. Datasets built with models whose terms restrict using their outputs to train other models are excluded, even when the dataset itself carries a permissive licence. The report names OpenAI’s proprietary GPT models, Anthropic’s Claude and Meta’s Llama as examples.
The corpus table lists scholarly and public sources individually, including KAKEN (Japan’s grants database), arXiv, peS2o, patents, and PDFs and HTML from WARP, the National Diet Library’s web archive, each with its release level.
The NII’s media advisory of 15 October announces the second Open LLM Symposium for 5 November in Tokyo, with EuroLLM lead André Martins (Instituto Superior Técnico, Lisbon) among the keynotes. The symposium is part of a programme funded by Japan’s education and science ministry (MEXT) on transparency and reliability of generative AI models (NII media advisory, PDF).
For a licensing desk, the release-level table is a ready-made template. Separating training, retrieval and display and redistribution into three explicit permissions is exactly the distinction most content licences still blur. Asking an AI partner “which of the three do you need?” is a better opening than “may we discuss AI?”.
Japan - AI proposes, the expert verifies, the record remembers. The Humanitext project led by Naoya Iwata (Nagoya University and NII), with colleagues at J.F. Oberlin University, the University of Tokyo and NII, is one of 19 projects chosen from 501 proposals in 42 countries for Schmidt Sciences’ Humanities and AI Virtual Institute. The grant is US$816,667 over three years, October 2026 to September 2029 (Schmidt Sciences, 14 Oct; NII release, 15 Oct).
The method is the part to copy. A language model proposes candidate links between classical texts, such as quotation, allusion, paraphrase or critique. Experts and graduate students accept, correct or reject each one. Verified links are stored with their type, direction, confidence and verification history in Wikibase and Neo4j, and then used as grounding for GraphRAG answers, which will be tested against ordinary retrieval-augmented generation. The researchers first build 500 relations by hand as a benchmark, aim for more than 10,000 verified relations in three years, and plan to release the graph, annotation software and benchmarks under open licences. It builds on Humanitext Antiqua, a research platform, public since August 2024, that answers questions about more than 2,300 Greek and Latin works by pointing to the source passages.
For cataloguers this is a familiar workflow wearing new clothes: machine suggestion, human decision, recorded provenance. If you want to run the same pattern on subject indexing or authority links, the minimum record per decision is short: proposed_by (model and version), decided_by (person and role), decision (accept / modify / reject), basis (the passage or source consulted) and timestamp. Keep it, and the next audit takes an afternoon instead of a quarter.
China - integrity talks and a standard still in the queue. In her letter of 12 October, COPE Chair Nancy Chescheir reports that after a June delegation to Beijing at the invitation of the Society of China University Journals, COPE is setting up an ad hoc group to address research and publication integrity concerns together with Chinese colleagues. Co-Vice Chair Tim Kersjes now leads COPE’s work on AI and external liaison (COPE, 12 Oct). The national guidance document on AIGC usage boundaries in academic publishing that we noted last week still shows as at the approval stage (正在批准) in the national standards register when we checked on 18 October (project 20253114-Z-469).
India, Singapore and elsewhere. We found no new primary-source development this week for India: the NIRF retraction story we covered on 12 October has not moved on in any official source we could find. We also found nothing solid from Singapore or other BRICS members for this desk, and we say so rather than pad.
Noted this week
Not a method. Seven signals from the sources above:
Agents are tools, not scientists - the fourth ERA Living Guidelines add checkpoints for AI agents, a “substantial use” line for disclosure, and a warning about hidden prompts in metadata.
Publishers pledge to RAISE - Elsevier (licences, about €1m a year in-kind) and Frontiers (AI-ready curation for 1,000 Horizon Europe datasets) are among the first seven pledgers; delivery is reviewed annually.
ONIX Issue 75 - a content audience and a resource type for LLM training, JSON as a file format, and manuscript submission and acceptance dates for scholarly books. The payload format comes from the German ONIX group.
Evidence before scale - a Scholarly Kitchen guest post asks publishers to measure what AI changes and to share inconclusive results.
Rights levels in the open - LLM-jp-4 separates training, retrieval and redistribution for every dataset; a usable template for licence talks.
Verified, not just generated - Humanitext stores each AI-proposed link with an expert’s decision and its verification history.
Calendar - the ISC, COPE, STM and Global Young Academy disclosure consultation closed on 16 October, with a draft “Vancouver Standard” to be refined in round three, end of 2026 to early 2027 (ISC); COPE expects the fifth Principles of Transparency at the end of October; Crossref meets on 22 October.

title: The 2016 MARC21 core set for e-resources, updated
description: DataMercs' core set for MARC records, brought up to current practice and widened to e-journals and databases. One table, three markets: DNB and the German-language union catalogues, LC/PCC, and OCLC. Draft.

The 2016 core set is my core field set for e-book MARC records: which fields a publisher’s record has to carry so that libraries in Germany and the US can load it without rework. Its last revision dates from December 2016. This page brings it up to date and widens it to e-journals and databases.


It is a delivery core, not a cataloguing manual. Each column says what one document asks for, in its own layer. Where a document does not mention a field, the cell says so and nothing more.

DNB / DACH = the AG KVA requirements of the German-language networks and the DNB for e-book deliveries (they cover e-books; e-journals run through the ZDB). LC / PCC = the PCC Provider-Neutral guide, falling back to the BSR or CSR where it is silent (marked). OCLC = Bibliographic Formats and Standards input standards.Applicability. ● core for that resource type · ○ if applicable · – not applicable.DataMercs core. Rows named DataMercs core are decisions of this set that go beyond the three market documents. DataMercs extension marks a use that MARC 21 does not define as such.Links. Every tag opens its MARC 21 Bibliographic page at the Library of Congress. BFAS opens the OCLC page for the same field.

Contents note: 505 alongside the 856 TOC link

DataMercs core Wherever a table of contents exists, e-books and edited volumes carry it as text in 505. A full-text contents note turns every chapter title, and in the enhanced form every chapter author, into a search and index entry point. A link in 856 42 $3 Table of contents gives one URL that most catalogues do not index. 505 complements the 856 link; it does not replace it. Send both when you have both.

505  00 $t Introduction / $r A. Editor -- $t Records in transit / $r B. Author $g (pages 11–38) -- $t Identifiers that hold / $r C. Author and D. Author --
505  80 $t Licences in the record / $r E. Author -- $t Index.

505 0# basic: all parts in a single $a, separated by --. Use it for monographs, or when only chapter titles are available.
505 00 enhanced: each part as $t title, $r statement of responsibility (after /) and $g other information such as part, volume or page numbering. Use it for edited volumes and multi-author works where chapter authors matter: systems can index $t and $r for title and author searches. They are not controlled headings; chapter authors who need authority control also get a 700 (or 730/740 for titles).
Indicators (LoC): first 0 contents, 1 incomplete, 2 partial, 8 no display constant; second # basic, 0 enhanced.
Punctuation: -- between parts, / before a statement of responsibility; end the field with a full stop unless the contents continue in another 505.
Long contents: 505 is repeatable. Split a long table of contents over several 505 fields: the first carries first indicator 0, each continuation carries 8, so no second “Contents:” label is displayed. OCLC BFAS shows exactly this (505 80 continuing the note begun in the first). bd505 · BFAS 505

What the current documents ask for
Each document works on its own layer: a cataloguing rule (how to describe), an application profile (which elements a programme requires), or a delivery spec (what a supplier must send). The summaries below say which layer, then what matters for an e-resource record.
DNB and the German-language union catalogues
AG KVA, Anforderungen der deutschsprachigen Verbundsysteme und der Deutschen Nationalbibliothek an Metadatenlieferungen zu E-Books und E-Book-Paketen (English: Metadata for e-books). Current online edition, valid from 1 June 2023; it replaces the PDF edition of 5 August 2016 (“überarbeitete Fassung für die Anwendung des Regelwerkes RDA ab 1. Oktober 2015”, PDF). Delivery spec of the networks and the DNB (BVB, DNB, GBV, hbz, hebis, KOBV, OBV, SLSP, SWB, ZDB). MARC 21 (ISO 2709 or MARCXML) or ONIX 3.0.8, UTF-8, SFTP or OAI-PMH. Each element is marked mandatory, mandatory if available, or optional, with a MARC field and example. Key MARC points: 001 stable ID; 003/040 $a provider; 020, 024 $2 doi, 776 08 $i Erscheint auch als $n Druck-Ausgabe $z; 1XX/7XX with $4 and $0; 506 0# $a Open access; 540 $a $f $2 cc $u; 912/950 for collections. KBART title lists go alongside. German · English
RDA DACH. Cataloguing rule and application profile for the region, on the STA documentation platform since 2023; release 2026/1 came out in June 2026. It merges RDA, the former D-A-CH application rules and the explanations. sta.dnb.de/doc/RDA
DNB MARC 21 field descriptions. Format application: how the DNB itself exports title, holdings and authority data. Title data are at version 4.4 (10 November 2025). dnb.de/marc21
K10plus (GBV and SWB). MARC 21 export documentation of the shared catalogue, and its cataloguing manual for e-books. MARC21 export · E-books manual (PDF)
Library of Congress and PCC (US)
PCC Provider-Neutral E-Resource MARC Record Guide (P-N/RDA combined, 30 September 2024). Application guideline for one record per e-resource across providers: monographs, serials and integrating resources. 040 $e rda $e pn; no package or provider-specific data in 773, 8XX, 506 or 540; 506 and 856 $7 0 for open access. Guidelines page · PDF
BIBCO Standard Record (BSR) RDA MAP (26 April 2024). Application profile, a floor record for monographs. Textual monographs: LDR/17 blank, LDR/18 i or c, at least one class number, subject and genre/form access supported by authority records. BSR MAPs
CONSER Standard Record (CSR) RDA MAP. Application profile for serials: 310 frequency core if known, always a source-of-title and “Description based on” note in 588. CSR (PDF)
LC-PCC Policy Statements. Policy layer on top of RDA, free in the RDA Toolkit. Access
Official RDA. PCC moves to the official RDA Toolkit on a rolling schedule (May 2024 to April 2027). Until PCC says otherwise, PCC records follow original RDA. PCC notice (PDF) · FAQ
OCLC
Bibliographic Formats and Standards (BFAS). Input standard. Two levels: Full (ELvl blank or 1) and Minimal (ELvl 7). Every field page gives Full/Minimal for the field and each subfield. Introduction · Fixed fields
Vendor Record Contribution Program. Delivery acceptance spec for supplier records: valid MARC 21 (or MARCXML, ONIX 3.0+), fewer than 2% machine-detectable coding errors, US cataloguing and heading standards, at least minimal-level completeness. VRCP
WorldShare Collection Manager, knowledge base MARC delivery. Delivery spec on the library side: a title gets a record only with an OCLC number, a format, a coverage value and, for e-books and full-text journals, a title URL. That makes the KBART title_url and a WorldCat match part of the record supply. Troubleshooting

The 505 is core here because the book has a table of contents; it uses the enhanced form because the introduction has its own author. The 500, the 520–883 link and the 650–883 link are conditional: use them only when AI was involved. The record CC0 line goes on every record. XX-0000 stands in for your MARC organisation code or ISIL.
Reference for a well-received OA e-book data sample: OA e-book collection, public metadata portal.
For a DACH delivery, swap the 776 for 776 08 $i Erscheint auch als $n Druck-Ausgabe $z …, add the RSWK chain as 689 00 $a … $0 (DE-588)… if the recipient wants it, and use 084 for RVK or BK. A traced series takes 490 1# plus 830 #0.
Provenance and licensing: the DataMercs layer
The three market documents stop at the resource. This set also says who may reuse the record and how a machine was involved in the work or the metadata. Each standard below is named by its layer.
CC0 on the record itself

DataMercs core Every record carries a CC0 statement for its own metadata. This is separate from the resource licence in 506/540. Reason: anyone can reuse, merge and enrich the record without asking.

540  ## $3 Bibliographic record $a Metadata in this record released under CC0 1.0 Universal. $f CC0 1.0 $2 cc $u https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/ $q XX-0000
MARC 21 field 540 (format, LoC, December 2024): terms governing use and reproduction. $f takes a term from a standardised list such as Creative Commons. $2 cc is the Creative Commons code in the LoC Access Restriction Term Source Codes. $u takes a URI. $q names the supplying agency. LoC’s own CC example puts the licence URI in $0 (added 2024); this set uses $u, as the DNB does in its resource 540. bd540 · source codes
The extension. 540 $3 is defined as “part of the described material”. Using it to point at the bibliographic record is a DataMercs extension. MARC 21 has no field for the licence of the record itself, and the MARC papers on open access and licences (2018-DP11, Proposal 2019-01, 2024-DP04) deal with the resource. Put the record line after the resource 540 so that a system ignoring $3 still shows the resource licence first. 2019-01 · 2024-DP04
DNB (policy layer): all title data and GND authority data are available under CC0 1.0, stated on the business-model page and in the open-data download notes. The licence is not repeated in the records; live records carry 540 only for the resource (540 ## $u http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0 $2 cc). Geschäftsmodell · data.dnb.de
OCLC (policy layer): OCLC recommends the Open Data Commons Attribution licence (ODC-BY) for member libraries that publish WorldCat-derived data, with an attribution sentence and a pointer to the WorldCat community norms. The terms live in WorldCat Rights and Responsibilities; origin travels in the record as 040 and the 035 (OCoLC) number. Press release, 6 August 2012 · WorldCat Rights and Responsibilities
AI in the resource
COPE and ICMJE (publication-ethics layer): an AI tool cannot be an author because it cannot take responsibility for the work. Authors disclose the tool and how they used it. COPE · ICMJE
MARC relator list (code list, LoC): it has no term or code for AI or machine generation. The nearest entries, software developer [swd] and music programmer [mup], describe persons. Relator terms
CRediT (ANSI/NISO Z39.104-2022, contributor-role taxonomy): its 14 roles describe human contributors. The STM classification of AI use in manuscript preparation (September 2025) names the activities, such as language editing or drafting, that a disclosure can cite. The AID Framework (2024) gives a structured disclosure statement. CRediT · STM · AID Framework
So the disclosure is a note, not a heading. 500 fits: it is the general note for information without a specialised 5XX. 545 holds the creator’s biography, and 588 is about the record.
500  ## $a AI use disclosed by the author: language editing of chapters 2–4 with a generative AI tool; the author reviewed all text.
If the tool has to be indexed, an uncontrolled added entry can trace it. This is a DataMercs extension, optional, and never a 100/700:
720  2# $a Example language model 1.0 $e language editing tool
AI in the record
MARC 21 field 883 (format, LoC, May 2020) records metadata provenance for a linked field. First indicator: 0 fully machine-generated, 1 partially machine-generated, 2 not machine-generated, # no information. Subfields:
$a creation process
$c confidence value, from 0 to 1, with a point or comma
$d creation date (yyyymmdd)
$q agency, as a MARC organisation code
$u URI of the process
$x validity end date
$w source record number
$0 source authority number, $1 real-world object URI
$8 field link
Link both fields with the same $8 number and link type p.
520  3# $8 1\p $a [abstract text]
650  #7 $8 2\p $a [subject] $0 (DE-588)… $2 gnd

XX-0000 is a placeholder for your MARC organisation code or ISIL. DNB records use the same pattern for machine-assigned DDC classes, for example 883 0# $8 6\p $a emakn $c 0,16014 $d … $q DE-101 $u https://d-nb.info/provenance/plan#emakn. bd883 · $8 link types
Data provenance $7 (MARC 21 Appendix J, added 2022, revised December 2025) is defined in 520, 650, 500 and 720, among others, but not in 540 or 883. It holds a provenance value for the other subfields of the same field and can carry a category code from the LoC Data Provenance Code List, for example dpenmw (note on metadata work). The values themselves are not controlled. Use it as an optional in-field echo; 883 stays the carrier. Appendix J · Code list
520  3# $a [abstract text] $7 (dpenmw)machine-generated, human-reviewed
A human-readable line in 588 is also within that field’s scope (“tracking and controlling the metadata”): 588 ## $a Abstract machine-generated and reviewed by the cataloguer.
Why
Provenance is the point of this site. A record that says who made it, by which process and under which licence can be trusted, corrected and passed on. This page practises what it describes: it names its author of record and its tool, credited as “OSDS AI, via Grok Bot”, which is a disclosure and not an authorship. title: Move with the times: the ALA's refusal is contract language
description: The ALA Guidance on the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Libraries treats delay and non-adoption as professional outcomes, not failures. A reading for the metadata desk, the systems office and the consortial buyer: which sentences can go straight into vendor clauses and local procedure. Efficiency gains should ease overburdened staff through upskilling and hybridization, not become a reason for reductions.
contents:
Source. American Library Association. Guidance on the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Libraries➚.
Prepared by the ALA Artificial Intelligence Policy Working Group for libraries drafting or revising local AI policies, procedures and vendor-review practice. Built on the ALA Core Values, with an appendix ethics framework after Luciano Floridi. Accessed 14 October 2026.
The short version
This autumn there is no shortage of mood about AI in libraries. This document is not mood. It is operational text: decision points, review questions and a vocabulary of outcomes that a library, a press or a consortium can write straight into procedure.
Our beat is the part of the stack where AI arrives as a default rather than a decision: the discovery layer, the cataloguing client, the acquisitions platform, the assistant quietly switched on in a release note. For that desk the guidance does three useful things. It names refusal as a legitimate outcome of review. It leaves final authority over metadata with the people who have the expertise. And it hands procurement a checklist that, with very little editing, reads like contract language.
We do not read it as a brake. We want AI in cataloguing, discovery and scholarly publishing wherever there is a documented public-service purpose and the safeguards exist, not least where it can ease the load on already overburdened staff through deliberate upskilling and hybrid roles. So does the guidance. What it adds is the paper trail: the thing that makes responsible adoption defensible, and that stops efficiency being quietly converted into headcount reduction.
Refusal as an affirmative choice
The sentence that matters most is short:

“A considered decision to delay, omit, remove, or discontinue use of a product is an affirmative professional choice grounded in library values, not a failure of adoption.”

The outcomes listed around it deserve copying into local procedure verbatim:
adoption, limited use, pilot testing, delay, pause, non-adoption, removal or discontinuation.
Eight states, not two. Adoption or limited use requires a documented service benefit and adequate safeguards; the rest apply when policy, vendor controls, staffing or review cannot mitigate the risks.
This moves the burden of proof in a renewal meeting: The question is no longer “why aren’t you using the feature?” but “has anyone documented the benefit and the safeguards?”
If nobody has, the outcome is delay, and delay is a professional position.
That matters for colleagues whose training never covered model evaluation, data-processing agreements or ranking audits. Their worry is real, and it is not a character flaw. The guidance itself asks that AI literacy work avoid shaming anyone who is curious, sceptical, obliged to use it or trying to avoid it. A named outcome called “delay” gives those colleagues defensible ground while they acquire what the hybrid role demands.
Where we would refuse outright is narrower: labour removed with no plan for upskilling or reinvestment, provenance vanishing upstream, the catalogue treated as scrap, a privacy failure that cannot be mitigated.
The guidance covers each. It does not ask anyone to refuse everything else.
What the metadata desk can lift
Human in the loop, as a requirement. The technical-services line is unambiguous: AI applied to “cataloging, classification, and acquisitions processes must include human-in-the-loop configuration and oversight including full control to accept, edit, or reject suggestions.”
A client that writes suggestions straight into the record, or lets you accept but not edit, does not meet it.
Final authority stays with expertise. AI may assist with draft descriptions, candidate terms, metadata enrichment and first-pass classification. Final authority stays with staff who hold cataloguing, language, cultural, subject or community expertise, explicitly for subject headings, classification, authority work, non-English and non-Latin-script materials, local history, community materials and sensitive topics. The guidance also asks local procedures to define review methods, sampling, escalation, documentation and error correction. And it notes something every cataloguer has felt: automation shifts the decision to the end of the task, which is the worst possible place for a subject heading.
Keep the boring paths. Alongside AI-enhanced discovery, libraries should preserve “predictable, transparent, non-personalized, and explainable access paths”: known-item search, subject browsing, chronological lists. If the controlled-vocabulary browse breaks when the ranking model is switched on, your metadata investment has been quietly demoted.
Vendor review as clause text. The privacy section lists what vendor review should establish: whether AI features are on by default; whether the library can switch them off; what data the system collects; whether prompts, searches, account activity, reference interactions or staff inputs are logged; whether data are used for model training or product improvement; where data are stored; which subprocessors are involved; retention; deletion; and audit or exit rights. In plain language. Each item converts directly into an RFP question or a licence schedule. Two neighbouring lines strengthen the buyer’s hand: libraries “must not be required to trade data control for access to AI functionality”, and vendors should offer equivalent non-AI services or document the limitation and name alternatives.
Collections and labour: upskilling and hybrid roles
On collections the guidance is plain: declining to acquire primarily AI-generated materials is a legitimate exercise of professional judgement and fiscal stewardship when they fall short of local standards for quality, accuracy, originality, transparency or community relevance. Presses should read that the other way round: disclosure of AI assistance is becoming a selection criterion.
On labour it is equally plain, and the sensible response is affirmative rather than defensive. Libraries should not use AI to justify staff reductions, deskilling or the replacement of professional judgement. Verified efficiency gains belong in working conditions and services. The guidance asks libraries to define meaningful human review (who reviews, with what training, when, and with what authority to question, correct, reject or escalate) and to use technology to extend staffing capacity, support training and empower library workers.
With many technical-services teams already stretched, the useful reading is that AI should be embraced precisely to ease that load, provided the recovered capacity goes into upskilling and hybrid roles rather than being booked as spare headcount. Cataloguers and metadata specialists become reviewers and auditors of AI suggestions, designers of sampling regimes, owners of escalation paths and keepers of the error log. Routine first-pass work shrinks; the judgement that remains is applied at higher leverage, backed by explicit training. Delay stays available while that training and the local procedures are built. Review that nobody is paid for, or that is simply piled onto a full workload, is not review.
The framing also accommodates the range of technical comfort in the profession. Colleagues who already treat systems work as core expertise can lead the hybrid design; colleagues whose professional identity rests on collections, community or reading can stand on the named outcome of delay while they acquire the competencies. The instruction to shame neither group still applies.
Homework for practitioners
Concrete enough for this week:
Map the stack. List every AI-enabled feature in your discovery layer, library system, cataloguing client and publishing platform. Note which are on by default and whether you can switch them off.
Write three questions into the next renewal. Are prompts, searches or logs used for training or product improvement? Is there an equivalent non-AI path? What audit and exit rights do we have?
Name the human in the loop. For cataloguing and classification suggestions: who accepts, edits or rejects; at what sampling rate; where escalation goes; where errors are logged. Include the training those people will receive.
Test the boring paths. Confirm that known-item search, subject browse and chronological lists still behave predictably with AI ranking switched on.
Add one line to collection policy on primarily AI-generated materials: accept, case by case, or decline, with quality and disclosure criteria.
Document the gap. If you cannot get a plain-language answer on data use, write that down and record delay as the outcome until you do. The guidance says as much: if you cannot determine how a system uses data, delay, limit, refuse or discontinue. Record, too, whether any efficiency gain is earmarked for upskilling or service improvement rather than absorbed by the next round of cuts.
Close
Those who will not move with the times will be moved on by them. Acceleration with a paper trail is still acceleration. The ALA text says it is meant to evolve as the landscape changes, and it will. The useful part is already stable: a list of outcomes that includes no, a human entitled to say it, and a set of questions vendors can be asked to answer in writing. Used as intended, those tools let a library embrace AI to ease overburdened staff through deliberate hybrid roles, rather than as a pretext for cuts.
Reference
American Library Association, AI Policy Working Group. Guidance on the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Libraries. Accessed 14 October 2026.
https://www.ala.org/tools/standards-and-guidelines/guidance-use-artificial-intelligence-libraries➚

title: News wrap · 12 October 2026 - Provenance wants a payload
description: Weekly news wrap (not a workshop) for 12 October 2026. Publishers, NISO, COUNTER and Ithaka S+R launch TRACE so that AI answers can say where they came from; NISO republishes Journal Article Versions; a global AI-disclosure standard takes comments until 16 October; the Bodleian’s new AI policy comes with a cataloguing case where a human reads every AI suggestion; and India’s national university ranking scrutinises retracted papers and may bar repeat offenders.
contents:
Industry notes · news wrap · not a workshop


Week of 12 October 2026


A briefing of what to notice this week, with sources. How-to and cataloguing practice stay in separate posts - see Ghost in the MARC for the standards work.

Frankfurt week, and the scholarly-publishing trade spent it on one question: when an AI system hands a researcher an answer, can anyone tell where it came from?
At the STM Frankfurt Conference, publishers and standards bodies launched TRACE, a joint effort to make provenance, attribution and usage survive the trip through AI tools.
NISO, in the same week, republished its vocabulary for article versions. A global AI-disclosure standard is collecting comments until 16 October.
And on the library side, the Bodleian published an AI policy that reads less like a manifesto and more like a cataloguing rule.
The common thread is old courier wisdom: the package is only as good as the label that stays on it.
TRACE: three projects, one question
What launched. TRACE - Trusted Retrieval & Attribution for Content Ecosystems was presented on stage at the STM Frankfurt Conference by Priya Madina (Springer Nature), Tasha Mellins-Cohen (COUNTER), Todd Toler (Ithaka S+R) and Todd Carpenter (NISO) (Scholarly Kitchen, 7 Oct; COUNTER, 6 Oct). STM’s own conference report describes it as an effort to keep trusted research “identifiable, attributable, and measurable as AI increasingly mediates access to information” (STM, 9 Oct).
It starts with funding for three parallel pieces of work:
How agents reach content. The Endpoint Question, a three-month study led independently by Ithaka S+R, will look at how AI agents discover scholarly content, authenticate through a user’s existing entitlements, receive provenance-bearing information and leave a credible record of use. Findings are to be published openly. Toler notes that publishers “are already exploring MCP endpoints” - the Model Context Protocol, a common way of plugging tools into AI assistants - one organisation at a time (STM announcement, 6 Oct).
What metadata travels with a source. NISO is launching a pilot, planned at up to twelve months, to define and test a minimum viable metadata model for provenance and attribution at inference time: the information that should accompany a source when an AI system retrieves, cites or transforms it.
It builds on existing pieces (W3C PROV, C2PA content credentials, DOIs and other persistent identifiers) and explicitly does not try to solve attribution inside model weights, copyright enforcement or access control (Scholarly Kitchen).
How AI usage gets counted. TRACE part-funds COUNTER’s work on the COUNTER API and JSON Schema for AI usage metrics. Phase two of that guidance is meant to cover inference-time use outside publishers’ own platforms, and a holistic “AI retrievals” metric is planned (COUNTER; Scholarly Kitchen).
Who is at the table. COUNTER lists the contributors to the funded development work: American Chemical Society, American Psychological Association, Cambridge University Press, Elsevier, IEEE, IOP Publishing, Sage, Springer Nature and Wiley (COUNTER).
That is a sensible coalition for getting things built, and also a coalition with an obvious interest in being credited. Neither fact cancels the other. The useful test for everyone else is whether the outputs stay open and implementable by a university press, a society journal or a repository with no developer on staff. The early signs are reasonable: Ithaka S+R will publish openly, and NISO says it has begun talking to Creative Commons about fitting a provenance package into CC Signals.
Why it matters at our counter. For librarians, the COUNTER line is the one to watch: COUNTER describes TRACE as aiming for a system where “libraries can see how the content they license is used”. If AI retrievals become a reportable metric, they will end up in renewal conversations.
For metadata leads, the NISO pilot is the quiet one with the long tail. A minimum provenance payload will be filled from the metadata we already ship. A reader comment under the Kitchen post put it plainly:
the provenance package “will only be as good as the metadata behind it”.
Uneven affiliations, missing licences and orphaned version links will not become trustworthy just because an agent repeats them politely.
Versions are provenance too: NISO JAV, revised
On 5 October, NISO published the revised Journal Article Versions Recommended Practice, NISO RP-8-2026, first issued with ALPSP in 2008. It updates the terms and definitions for article versions, gives guidance on carrying version information in machine-readable formats such as JATS, and adds worked examples.
It is freely available (NISO press release; JAV working group page).
Co-chair Patrick Hargitt (Olive Turn) gives the reason it belongs in this wrap:
readers need to know whether a work was reviewed, where it sits in its life cycle and whether it has changed, “and AI makes that clarity even more important”. Co-chair Mike Nason (University of New Brunswick) points at libraries, repositories and indexers, which all depend on consistent version information. The connection to TRACE is direct. A citation that cannot tell a preprint from a corrected version of record is not provenance; it is a rumour with a DOI.
The vocabulary waited eighteen years for its revision. The agents will not wait that long.
AI disclosure: one standard, comments close Friday
The International Science Council, COPE, STM and the Global Young Academy, with the World Conference on Research Integrity, are working towards a global reporting standard for AI disclosure in research, which its organisers compare to the way CRediT standardised contributor roles.
Round two of the consultation, on when AI use must be disclosed, where and how, and how to describe human oversight and verification, closes on 16 October 2026.
A refined “Vancouver Standard” is planned for late 2026 to early 2027 (ISC consultation page).
The working threshold from round one is worth reading slowly: AI use should be disclosed if it “substantively shapes or replaces human judgement”, tested by whether a disciplinary peer “would reasonably need to know” about it to assess the work (SARUA summary). The draft questions also ask whether disclosures should name which human checked each AI use, and whether prompts or logs should be kept.
Why a metadata desk should care: machines already read these statements. In a new Crossref series on tools that use its API, Crossref reports more than 100 million REST API requests from Grobid clients in the first quarter of 2026, and notes that Grobid recently added extraction of CRediT and conflict-of-interest statements (Crossref, 6 Oct). An AI-use statement that is structured can be harvested; one that is free prose in an acknowledgement will mostly be lost in extraction. If your press or library has a view on structure, this is the week to send it.
Library desk: the Bodleian’s worked case puts a human on every suggestion
The Bodleian Libraries’ AI Policy, dated 29 September 2026, sets out eight principles after a year of consultation and covers the description of collections and metadata explicitly.
Two lines stand out for practitioners: “We will refrain from treating AI adoption as an objective in itself”, and, where appropriate, users get an option to opt out of AI use.
The policy is to be reviewed annually (policy PDF).
A companion post on 1 October walks through hypothetical use cases, and the cataloguing one is among the most concrete AI rules we have seen from a large research library this year. A cataloguer drafting descriptions and subject terms for an out-of-copyright pamphlet backlog with an approved chatbot reads every suggestion; “nothing is published automatically”; offensive historical terminology picked up from the source is rewritten and flagged to the team; and a note in the project file records that the records were drafted with AI assistance and reviewed by staff before publication (Bodleian Digital blog).
This is acceleration with a seatbelt, which is the version we can support. One question for the next revision: the note sits in the project file. Whether it should also travel in the record itself, where an aggregator or an agent can see it, is exactly the kind of decision TRACE and the disclosure standard will eventually force on everyone.
Global desk: India counts retractions; China and Japan tighten the pipes
India - rankings meet retraction data. India’s National Institutional Ranking Framework (NIRF) rankings for 2026 had not appeared by 7 October, although they normally come out in August or September. ThePrint reports that the National Board of Accreditation, which runs the exercise for the Ministry of Education, has flagged a large number of retracted papers during this year’s assessment and, according to unnamed officials, is considering barring repeat offenders from future rankings (ThePrint, 6 Oct; India Today, 7 Oct).
The mechanism is not new: the official India Rankings 2025 report confirms that negative marking for retracted publications was introduced last year in the Overall, Engineering, Universities and Research Institutions categories (NIRF 2025 report). Citing Retraction Watch data, ThePrint puts India at 887 retractions in 2025, second only to China at 1,701.
Note what this means for metadata: once retraction status feeds a national ranking, a missing or late retraction notice is no longer a housekeeping issue. It moves an institution’s score. ThePrint also notes that a retraction does not by itself mean misconduct, and a ranking that cannot tell an honest correction from a paper mill will reward silence.
China - retractions, and an AI-content standard in the queue. At a State Council Information Office press conference on 29 September, Vice Minister of Science and Technology Qiu Yong said the ministry is leading a special campaign on papers retracted for academic misconduct and pushing the relevant authorities to set up routine checking and handling of retracted papers within their own systems, alongside a database of serious research-integrity violations used in grant, academy and award vetting (Science and Technology Daily).
Separately, a national standardisation guidance document, Guideline on the boundaries of AIGC usage in academic publishing (学术出版中人工智能生成合成内容（AIGC）使用边界指南), drafted under the national technical committee for information and documentation (TC4), with the Institute of Scientific and Technical Information of China, Tsinghua University Press and Wanfang Data among the drafters, is listed in the national standards register as at the approval stage when we checked on 11 October (national standards platform, project 20253114-Z-469).
Not this week’s news, but one to watch: when it is published, China will have a national reference for AI-generated content in academic publishing while the global disclosure standard is still in consultation.
Japan - the PDF era gets an end date. J-STAGE, the Japan Science and Technology Agency’s national journal platform, has decided that full-text JATS-XML will be mandatory for new research articles in journals from fiscal year 2029 (Reiwa 11), with the transition expected to finish by the end of March 2030. The decision sits in the April 2026 “deliberation summary” of the J-STAGE Advisory Committee on the revised medium- to long-term strategy (J-STAGE strategy decisions, April 2026).
Scope is narrow on purpose: only journals and only research-article types. Editorials, announcements, columns and abstract-only items stay exempt. Already-published articles and retrospective deposits of back issues remain PDF-only.
PDF itself is not abolished; it becomes optional, and a lag of up to six months between the XML and the PDF (in either order) is allowed.
What ends is the long habit of depositing new research articles as PDF plus bibliographic XML and calling that complete. From fiscal 2029 the required object is structured full-text JATS; the paginated file is the optional rendering.
The minimum tagging bar is deliberately modest and stays inside the JATS 1.1 profile J-STAGE already accepts (its own DTD based on the NISO Publishing tag set):
An article needs the ordinary front / body / back structure; the body must be sectioned; floats must carry titles and sit near their reference or be internally linked; tables and maths are preferably structured text but images remain acceptable.
No change to the underlying JATS version is planned. Current uptake is low - presentations in 2026 put full-text XML at roughly 7.6 % of current J-STAGE journals, against near-universal use among major Western publishers and earlier mandates at SciELO.
The usual barriers are staff, money and time; the free Word/LaTeX-to-XML conversion tool offered since 2020 is still little used.
Further GUI work and an XML-to-PDF generator are scheduled for around March 2027. InDesign is not supported and is not planned to be.
JST lists several reasons. Machine readability for AI use is one of them, but not the only one: better on-platform HTML reading, translation, text-to-speech, search, external reuse and international circulation are given equal weight.
An online seminar tracing the forty-year road to the mandate (XSPA president Hidehiko Nakanishi, co-hosted with JEPA) is set for 6 November (XSPA summary, 25 Sep; JEPA, 7 Oct).
For a metadata desk the practical point is straightforward. From 2030 a large slice of Japanese society-journal content will arrive as structured JATS rather than PDF-plus-bibliographic XML. That changes what can be harvested, indexed, versioned and attributed without OCR or layout reconstruction - exactly the layer TRACE and the revised NISO JAV are trying to keep intact once agents start mediating access. The package, again, is only as good as the label that stays on it.
Elsewhere. At STM Frankfurt, South Africa’s Daan du Toit (Department of Science and Innovation) warned that “decoupling is dangerous for everyone”, and a China panel with Tsinghua University Press and the National Science Library of the Chinese Academy of Sciences discussed the shift from quantity-driven assessment towards quality and integrity (STM report). We found nothing solid from Singapore for this desk this week, and say so rather than pad.
Noted this week
Not a method. Seven signals from the sources above:
TRACE - publishers, NISO, COUNTER and Ithaka S+R launch a joint push to keep provenance, attribution and usage intact through AI tools.
Minimum provenance payload - NISO’s pilot will decide what metadata must travel with a source at inference time. What we ship today is what it will carry.
JAV revised - NISO RP-8-2026 gives article versions a current vocabulary and a machine-readable route via JATS.
AI disclosure - the ISC, COPE, STM and Global Young Academy consultation on a global reporting standard closes 16 October.
Bodleian - in its worked cataloguing case, a human reads every AI suggestion, nothing publishes automatically, and the use is noted.
Retractions as a score - India’s national ranking penalises them and may bar repeat offenders; China wants routine checking; retraction metadata is now policy input.
J-STAGE ends PDF-only - from fiscal 2029 structured JATS becomes the required object for new journal research articles; PDF turns optional.
Noted this week.
Sources

Introducing TRACE - COUNTER Metrics, 6 Oct 2026.
STM and Ithaka S+R launch research project on the interface between scholarly content and AI - STM, 6 Oct 2026.
STM Frankfurt Conference 2026 report - STM, 9 Oct 2026.
NISO Publishes Revised Journal Article Versions (JAV) Recommended Practice - NISO, 5 Oct 2026; JAV working group page.
AI disclosure in research: towards a global reporting standard - International Science Council (round two closes 16 Oct 2026).
Searching for a common, global reporting standard for AI disclosure in research - SARUA (Walter Claassen).
How Grobid uses Crossref metadata to enrich bibliographic information - Crossref, 6 Oct 2026.

Slew of retracted research papers flagged in NIRF assessment - ThePrint, 6 Oct 2026; India Today follow-up, 7 Oct 2026.
India Rankings 2025 report - NIRF, Ministry of Education.
科技部副部长邱勇：持续打击买卖论文等违规行为 - Science and Technology Daily, 29 Sep 2026.
